context_blurb:
A rock, a puddle, the air and your own hand look nothing alike. Yet every one of them is built from particles far too small to see. Nobody can see these particles, but you can test for them with a ball, a syringe or a dish of seawater. The tests show that even things you cannot see, like air, are real stuff.

Scientists call that stuff matter. Matter is anything that has mass and fills up space. Air, steam and smoke all have mass and take up room, so all three are matter, even though they are hard to see or hold. Sunlight has no mass, so a beam of sunlight is not matter: light, like heat and sound, is a form of energy.

All ordinary matter, from the air to rocks, seawater and your body, is made of tiny particles called atoms. Your body is also built of living cells, but cells are not the smallest bits: every cell is itself made of atoms, and so are the crystals in a rock.

Atoms are tiny beyond belief: a single human hair is about a million atoms wide. Even a hard steel nail is made of particles far too small to see, packed so close that the nail looks like one smooth piece. Not even the strongest school microscope can show them, and there is no air in the tiny gaps between them.

How do we know air is matter? Weigh it. Weigh a basketball while it is flat, then pump it up and weigh it again. The full ball weighs a little more, because air has weight, and the pump has squeezed extra air inside. Many people think air weighs nothing, but the scale says otherwise.

Air takes up space, too. Press a thumb hard over the tip of a syringe that seems empty, then push the plunger. It goes in a little way, then will go no farther. The syringe was full of air all along, and the air trapped inside it, squeezed into less space, pushes back on the plunger. Lift the thumb, and the plunger slides all the way in as the air rushes out. Nothing was stuck: the trapped air did the pushing.

Particles can travel, too. You can smell a rose from across a room before your eyes even find it. The scent of roses is made of tiny particles that come off the roses and drift through the air into your nose. The air itself does not turn smelly: the scent's particles just mix in among the air's, too small to see but still matter.

Stir some salt into water, and soon it is gone from sight, while the water stays clear. The salt has broken up into particles far too small to see, and they have spread all through the water. It has not melted, since salt melts only when heated to about 800 degrees Celsius. The salt is still there: the water tastes of it, and the salt comes back when the water dries up.

Seawater shows the same thing in reverse. It looks clear, yet it holds salt in bits too small to see. Leave some in a shallow dish in the sun, and the water slowly rises into the air as water vapour. The salt cannot rise with the water, so it is left in the dish as white crystals. Salt-makers dry seawater in shallow ponds in just this way.
